text: Early blight on tomato often starts on older, lower leaves as small, round, brown spots. Larger spots can develop target-like rings, with yellow tissue around them. Severely affected leaves may turn brown and fall. Stems can develop dry brown lesions, and fruit can develop leathery dark spots with raised rings, often near the stem.
title: Early blight in tomato and potato

text: The UMN guide says early blight spreads more readily in wet weather, heavy dew, or high humidity. Lower leaves can become infected when contaminated soil splashes onto them. Spores may also spread by wind, people, or equipment. The disease can persist in infected plant debris and soil.
title: Early blight in tomato and potato

text: For home gardens, UMN recommends using mulch to reduce soil splashing, watering at the base of the plant, and improving airflow by staking or trellising and spacing plants. The guide also describes resistant varieties as a way to reduce damage; resistance does not mean the plant cannot become infected.
title: Early blight in tomato and potato

text: The UMN guide recommends removing spotted leaves, cleaning hands and pruning tools after handling infected plants, and keeping leaves dry. It says not to remove more than one-third of the plant’s leaves. The guide also says most home gardeners do not need to use fungicide for early blight.
title: Early blight in tomato and potato

text: Tomato late blight can cause large, dark-brown leaf blotches with green-gray edges. Spots are not limited by the leaf’s major veins, and infection can spread through leaflets and leaf stems. Tomato fruit can develop firm, dark-brown spots. In humid conditions, thin white growth may appear on infected leaves, stems, or fruit.
title: Late blight of tomato and potato

text: Late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, which UMN describes as a water mold. The disease favors cool, damp conditions. The guide says infected transplants or windblown spores can introduce it, and that under cool, wet conditions it can spread rapidly.
title: Late blight of tomato and potato

text: For home gardens, UMN recommends regular scouting, removing diseased leaves, keeping foliage dry, watering at the base, and spacing or staking plants to improve airflow. It recommends rotating tomatoes away from related crops for three to four years. The guide notes that resistant varieties may still show symptoms and that pesticide sprays are not recommended for Minnesota home gardens.
title: Late blight of tomato and potato

text: The USU guide recommends growing tomatoes in a sunny spot with well-drained soil. Tomatoes do poorly in heavy, wet soil; the guide suggests a raised bed where drainage is poor. It also recommends using a soil test to decide whether fertilizer is needed. The guide is written for Utah, so its local planting schedules and measurements may not fit every region.
title: How to Grow Tomatoes in Your Garden

text: For tomato watering, the USU guide recommends watering deeply and regularly, using drip irrigation if possible. It says mulch can help conserve soil moisture and that irregular watering can contribute to blossom-end rot. These are recommendations from a Utah guide; local watering needs vary with climate and soil.
title: How to Grow Tomatoes in Your Garden

text: The USU guide warns that over-fertilizing tomato plants can cause excess leaf growth and delay fruit set and maturity. It also describes using stakes or cages to support plants and keep ripening fruit off the ground. The specific fertilizer amounts in this guide are for its Utah context and should not be treated as universal instructions.
title: How to Grow Tomatoes in Your Garden
